## From outcomes to distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: concept -->

How do we move from the complete outcome to the particular property named in the research question?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The foundations module gave us a probability space $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb{P}\rangle$. But a linguistic outcome in $\Omega$ may be a complete token, utterance, or annotated tree, while the next analysis may need only its duration, case, or dependency length. How do we move from the complete outcome to the particular property named in the research question?

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd
:::

## From outcomes to distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/03-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: concept -->

More specifically, it is a measurable function from outcomes to values, so questions about those values correspond to events in $\mathcal F$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A random variable supplies this **outcome-to-value mapping (OVM)**. The OVM extracts a value without replacing the outcome that supports it. More specifically, it is a measurable function from outcomes to values, so questions about those values correspond to events in $\mathcal F$.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd
:::

## From outcomes to distributions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: math -->

If $\mathcal X_C$ is the set of case values attested under the declared filtering rule, its value space and sigma-algebra are

$$
\mathcal G_C\equiv 2^{\mathcal X_C}.
$$

::: {.notes}

If $\mathcal X_C$ is the set of case values attested under the declared filtering rule, its value space and sigma-algebra are

## From outcomes to distributions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: math -->

The distribution of $C$ assigns $B$ the probability

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\in B)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}\!\left(C^{-1}(B)\right).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Now take any set of case values $B\in\mathcal G_C$. The event we can assign probability to is the set of pronoun outcomes that $C$ sends into $B$, that is, the preimage $C^{-1}(B)$. Thus the distribution of $C$ assigns $B$ the probability

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\in B)
\equiv
\mathbb{P}\!\left(C^{-1}(B)\right).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd
:::

## From outcomes to distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/07-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: concept -->

These conventions stay fixed throughout the module.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

As a function of $B$, this assignment is a probability measure on $\langle\mathcal X_C,\mathcal G_C\rangle$. We retain $\mathbb{P}$ for the probability measure on $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F\rangle$ and introduce no second measure symbol. Expressions such as $\mathbb{P}(C=c)$ abbreviate the corresponding preimage events. Lowercase $p$ and $q$ denote PMFs; lowercase $f$ and $g$ denote PDFs; uppercase $F$ and $G$ denote CDFs. These conventions stay fixed throughout the module.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd
:::

## Joint distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/index/12-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd; note-sha256: a05fc7e91ef909a273a5cf2a19de8b138f61673080e11a51222825305bda3c76; role: concept -->

These pages rely on the foundations definitions of joint event probability, conditional probability, and independence, so they give only working reminders of those ideas.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Finally, we move from one variable to several. A joint distribution preserves value pairings from the same outcome. Marginalization sums or integrates out one coordinate. Conditional independence states that one conditional distribution is invariant to an additional conditioning variable. Conditional expectation, covariance, and correlation summarize features of conditional or joint distributions. These pages rely on the foundations definitions of joint event probability, conditional probability, and independence, so they give only working reminders of those ideas.

[Sources]

## Why use random variables?

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/03-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: concept -->

How can we ask a probability question about that number while retaining the complete entry as the outcome?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The foundations chapter defined outcomes and sample spaces, events, and probability measures. An outcome in a pronunciation lexicon may be a complete entry containing an orthographic form, a pronunciation variant, and an ordered phone sequence. But a research question may concern only the number of phones. How can we ask a probability question about that number while retaining the complete entry as the outcome?

A random variable closes the gap by mapping a rich outcome to the particular value used in an analysis.

## The pronunciation-entry outcomes

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: concept -->

The data record gives the source checksum, preprocessing, and license.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We use the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (CMUdict) version 0.7b, a machine-readable pronunciation lexicon for US English developed for speech technology. The pinned source is distributed under CMU's permissive license, and the prepared teaching table retains every pronunciation entry and its ARPAbet phone sequence. It then deterministically counts all phones and vowel phones, identifying vowels from CMUdict's stress digits. The data record gives the source checksum, preprocessing, and license.

[Sources]

https://cmusphinx.github.io/2014/11/cmudict-0-7b-update/
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## The pronunciation-entry outcomes

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/06-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: concept -->

Every probability on this page describes uniform sampling from this pinned lexicon.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

One row is one dictionary pronunciation, not a word token in running speech. Alternate pronunciations of one orthographic form are separate, related rows, and CMUdict supplies no token frequencies. Thus every probability on this page describes uniform sampling from this pinned lexicon.

## One outcome can support several questions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/14-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: concept -->

The two mappings do not compete because they encode different questions about the same represented entry.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The same pronunciation can satisfy both $X(\omega)=x$ and $V(\omega)=v$. The two mappings do not compete because they encode different questions about the same represented entry.

## One outcome can support several questions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/15-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: concept -->

Replacing the entry with its count would remove those possibilities.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This separation matters because a stored linguistic record is usually richer than any one response. Keeping the outcome identifier, orthographic form, and phone sequence lets a later analysis study alternate pronunciations or particular phone patterns. Replacing the entry with its count would remove those possibilities.

## Why use random variables?: question 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/18-question; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: question -->

## Why use random variables?: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables/19-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f3805abbfe7becfa8c3328930337e7617b1897ff2e6074fc60bdad94d2dd536b; role: answer -->

Defining $C(\omega)$ as the consonant-phone count gives `all(cmu$phone_count == cmu$vowel_phone_count + cmu$consonant_phone_count)`, so $X=V+C$ for every entry.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Defining $C(\omega)$ as the consonant-phone count gives `all(cmu$phone_count == cmu$vowel_phone_count + cmu$consonant_phone_count)`, so $X=V+C$ for every entry.

Let $\langle\Omega,\mathcal F\rangle$ be the measurable space of pronunciation-entry outcomes, using the event space introduced earlier. Let $\langle\mathcal X,\mathcal G\rangle$ be the measurable space of nonnegative integer counts. The function has the form

V:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathcal X.

## Distinguishing the two spaces

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: concept -->

It does not mean that $v$ appeared in the observed resource, and it does not require that $v$ have positive probability.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The set $\mathcal X$ is the declared codomain of $V$, written $\operatorname{cod}(V)$. A statement such as $v\in\operatorname{cod}(V)$ refers to the declared value space. It does not mean that $v$ appeared in the observed resource, and it does not require that $v$ have positive probability.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

Here $q_{.5}$ is 2, and the preimage contains 61,493 entries.

::: {.notes}

This set is the **preimage** of $\{q_{.5}\}$ under $V$. Here $q_{.5}$ is 2, and the preimage contains 61,493 entries.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## Working backward with a preimage

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/11-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: concept -->

The preimage collects all of them.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The superscript $-1$ does not say that $V$ has an inverse function. Many pronunciation entries map to the same vowel count, so the count cannot recover one unique entry. The preimage collects all of them.

## Stating measurability {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/13-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: math -->

The function $V$ is a random variable when

$$
E\in\mathcal G
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The function $V$ is a random variable when

$$
E\in\mathcal G
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F.
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## Stating measurability

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/14-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: concept -->

It says that every measurable question about the value corresponds to a measurable event in the original outcome space.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This condition is called **measurability**. It says that every measurable question about the value corresponds to a measurable event in the original outcome space.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Stating measurability

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/15-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: concept -->

Otherwise the expression “the probability that a pronunciation has the median vowel count” would refer to an event to which the model assigns no probability.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $\{q_{.5}\}\in\mathcal G$, then the set of pronunciation entries in its preimage must belong to $\mathcal F$. Otherwise the expression “the probability that a pronunciation has the median vowel count” would refer to an event to which the model assigns no probability.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited
:::

## Stating measurability

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables/16-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/defining-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: cdffc9572fb3143d4e88f55230ae20cf565bf8c366586b54fd4dc474cf7237b2; role: concept -->

The requirement becomes more substantive for larger outcome spaces, but its interpretation remains the same.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In this finite empirical model, $\mathcal F\equiv2^\Omega$, so every preimage is measurable because every subset of pronunciation entries belongs to $\mathcal F$. The requirement becomes more substantive for larger outcome spaces, but its interpretation remains the same.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

## Finite and countably infinite sets

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/discrete-random-variables/09-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/discrete-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f9aca8eb5cf65b7945a8c9e2ec115e7a26193fcc7cdd13dba111060b7c0f8237; role: concept -->

*Countably infinite* means that every value can be assigned a position in a sequence even though the sequence has no final value.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

More specifically, a random variable is discrete when some finite or countably infinite set $\mathcal S$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(X\in\mathcal S)=1$. *Countably infinite* means that every value can be assigned a position in a sequence even though the sequence has no final value.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Finite and countably infinite sets

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/discrete-random-variables/10-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/discrete-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: f9aca8eb5cf65b7945a8c9e2ec115e7a26193fcc7cdd13dba111060b7c0f8237; role: concept -->

Both are discrete because their values occur as separate, listable possibilities.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The observed phone-count support is finite. The declared nonnegative-integer codomain is countably infinite. Both are discrete because their values occur as separate, listable possibilities.

## Probability mass functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/03-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: concept -->

Uniformly sampling one row gives each pronunciation entry the same mass; aggregating those row masses by `phone_count` produces an empirical probability mass function.

::: {.notes}

We answer this question with the empirical distribution over the CMUdict pronunciation entries introduced earlier. Uniformly sampling one row gives each pronunciation entry the same mass; aggregating those row masses by `phone_count` produces an empirical probability mass function.

## Probability mass functions {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: math -->

Basically, we need a lookup rule from values to probabilities. More specifically, the function assigning a probability to each codomain value is a **probability mass function**, abbreviated **PMF**. We write

$$
p_X:\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\to[0,1],
\qquad
p_X(x)\equiv\mathbb{P}(X=x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, we need a lookup rule from values to probabilities. More specifically, the function assigning a probability to each codomain value is a **probability mass function**, abbreviated **PMF**. We write

$$
p_X:\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\to[0,1],
\qquad
p_X(x)\equiv\mathbb{P}(X=x).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Probability mass functions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: math -->

For the empirical lexicon distribution with $N$ entries,

$$
\widehat p_X(x)
\equiv
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb 1\{X(\omega_i)=x\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the empirical lexicon distribution with $N$ entries,

## Checking the two PMF requirements {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/08-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: math -->

First, a PMF must assign nonnegative mass:

$$
p_X(x)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{cod}(X).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

First, a PMF must assign nonnegative mass:

$$
p_X(x)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{cod}(X).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Checking the two PMF requirements {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: math -->

Second, the masses across the codomain must sum to one:

$$
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}p_X(x)=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Second, the masses across the codomain must sum to one:

$$
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}p_X(x)=1.
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

The probability that $X$ exceeds its empirical third quartile is

$$

&=\sum_{\substack{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)\\x>q_{.75}}}p_X(x).
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

## Interpreting zero mass carefully

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions/14-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-mass-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 85fd5330ee0a3db23c583997388f91b348e2a105f54d2c4dbb1605f62f9f80ae; role: concept -->

It does not mean that no English pronunciation with that count can exist.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $p_X(x)=0$, then $X=x$ has zero probability under the stated empirical model. This may mean only that the count does not occur in the pinned lexicon. It does not mean that no English pronunciation with that count can exist.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

We use *continuous random variable* for the stronger, absolutely continuous case.

## A recorded value and a modeled point {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/continuous-random-variables/16-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/continuous-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: 9c259522a5971ba884cb9a30901ac9b105fc1843f9173d14fb5801f51467e4db; role: math -->

In the empirical distribution of the stored records, the value 240 ms has mass 0.022. Under an absolutely continuous model,

$$
\mathbb{P}(D=d)=0
$$

for every exact duration $d$, including the recorded median.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In the empirical distribution of the stored records, the value 240 ms has mass 0.022. Under an absolutely continuous model,

$$
\mathbb{P}(D=d)=0
$$

for every exact duration $d$, including the recorded median.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872
https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Applied_Probability_%28Pfeiffer%29/07%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions/7.01%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions

$$
\mathbb{P}(d-\varepsilon<D<d+\varepsilon)>0.

## Continuous random variables: answer 1

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/continuous-random-variables/20-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/continuous-random-variables.qmd; note-sha256: 9c259522a5971ba884cb9a30901ac9b105fc1843f9173d14fb5801f51467e4db; role: answer -->

## Probability density functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd; note-sha256: c52c9e68fe8694d5a88be3ec5204d3e3b63c82037eb04ee9a82a679e10db005a; role: concept -->

If individual points have zero probability, what quantity lets us recover the probability of an interval?

::: {.notes}

If individual points have zero probability, what quantity lets us recover the probability of an interval?

## Probability density functions {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd; note-sha256: c52c9e68fe8694d5a88be3ec5204d3e3b63c82037eb04ee9a82a679e10db005a; role: math -->

Basically, we describe how quickly probability accumulates near each value and compute interval probability as area. More specifically, a **probability density function**, abbreviated **PDF**, is a function $f_D:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\in A)=\int_A f_D(d)\,\mathrm dd
$$

for every measurable set $A$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, we describe how quickly probability accumulates near each value and compute interval probability as area. More specifically, a **probability density function**, abbreviated **PDF**, is a function $f_D:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\in A)=\int_A f_D(d)\,\mathrm dd
$$

for every measurable set $A$.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions/12-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd; note-sha256: c52c9e68fe8694d5a88be3ec5204d3e3b63c82037eb04ee9a82a679e10db005a; role: math -->

$$
f_D(d)\geq0

## Interpreting density in measurement units

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions/15-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd; note-sha256: c52c9e68fe8694d5a88be3ec5204d3e3b63c82037eb04ee9a82a679e10db005a; role: concept -->

Multiplying by an interval width in milliseconds cancels the units and produces a unitless probability.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The density $f_D(d)$ has units reciprocal to those of $D$. Because $D$ is measured in milliseconds, $f_D(d)$ is measured per millisecond. Multiplying by an interval width in milliseconds cancels the units and produces a unitless probability.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Interpreting density in measurement units

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions/16-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/probability-density-functions.qmd; note-sha256: c52c9e68fe8694d5a88be3ec5204d3e3b63c82037eb04ee9a82a679e10db005a; role: concept -->

The two objects have different units as well as different mathematical roles.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This unit check is another reason not to interpret density height as probability. The two objects have different units as well as different mathematical roles.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Cumulative distribution functions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 311f0380768ca7d9815655053b7e97a195feaaca06e74338b804cd1d5bac8a22; role: concept -->

A cumulative distribution function gives one threshold-based representation that applies to both.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The earlier pages represented discrete probability with a probability mass function and continuous probability with a probability density function. Must we switch representations every time we move between the two kinds of variable? A cumulative distribution function gives one threshold-based representation that applies to both.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Cumulative distribution functions {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 311f0380768ca7d9815655053b7e97a195feaaca06e74338b804cd1d5bac8a22; role: math -->

A **cumulative distribution function**, abbreviated **CDF**, records the probability at or below every threshold:

$$
F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],
\qquad
F_X(x)\equiv\mathbb{P}(X\leq x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **cumulative distribution function**, abbreviated **CDF**, records the probability at or below every threshold:

$$
F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],
\qquad
F_X(x)\equiv\mathbb{P}(X\leq x).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

The function accumulates probability from the lower end of the support through the threshold $x$.

## Accumulating a continuous density {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions/11-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 311f0380768ca7d9815655053b7e97a195feaaca06e74338b804cd1d5bac8a22; role: math -->

The probability in an interval above $a$ and at or below $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(a<X\leq b)
&=F_X(b)-F_X(a).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The probability in an interval above $a$ and at or below $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(a<X\leq b)
&=F_X(b)-F_X(a).
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Expected values {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd; note-sha256: d557e9ec371ee80261d16c08ff6e7c591080160b112b4714010642ea19bd65ac; role: math -->

The **expected value** weights each value by its probability. It is also called the mean of the distribution when the weighted average exists. For a discrete random variable,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
\equiv
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}x\,p_X(x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **expected value** weights each value by its probability. It is also called the mean of the distribution when the weighted average exists. For a discrete random variable,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
\equiv
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}x\,p_X(x).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Distribution-family calculations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values/13-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd; note-sha256: d557e9ec371ee80261d16c08ff6e7c591080160b112b4714010642ea19bd65ac; role: math -->

If $K\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(\pi)$ counts failures before the first success, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[K]
&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^k\pi\\
&=\pi(1-\pi)
  \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^{k-1}\\
&=\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $K\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(\pi)$ counts failures before the first success, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[K]
&=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^k\pi\\
&=\pi(1-\pi)
  \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k(1-\pi)^{k-1}\\
&=\frac{1-\pi}{\pi}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Distribution-family calculations {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values/14-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd; note-sha256: d557e9ec371ee80261d16c08ff6e7c591080160b112b4714010642ea19bd65ac; role: math -->

If $Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y]
&=\int_0^1
y\frac{y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\,\mathrm dy\\
&=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\\
&=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y]
&=\int_0^1
y\frac{y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\,\mathrm dy\\
&=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}\\
&=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Transforming first, then averaging {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 6ae2ba1f80af87020bfc2ae30229b70d8603436b9c6afbc5aaed3e23037c6d6a; role: math -->

For a discrete random variable, when $\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}|g(x)|p_X(x)<\infty$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
\equiv
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}g(x)p_X(x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a discrete random variable, when $\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}|g(x)|p_X(x)<\infty$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
\equiv
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}g(x)p_X(x).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd
:::

## Transforming first, then averaging {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 6ae2ba1f80af87020bfc2ae30229b70d8603436b9c6afbc5aaed3e23037c6d6a; role: math -->

For an absolutely continuous random variable, when $\int|g(x)|f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx<\infty$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
\equiv
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an absolutely continuous random variable, when $\int|g(x)|f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx<\infty$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
\equiv
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx.
$$

## Comparing two orders of operation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions/11-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd; note-sha256: 6ae2ba1f80af87020bfc2ae30229b70d8603436b9c6afbc5aaed3e23037c6d6a; role: math -->

Thus, for a nonlinear function $g$,

$$
g(\mathbb{E}[X])\neq\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
$$

in general.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The two operations answer different questions. $g(\mathbb{E}[X])$ transforms the center of the original values, whereas $\mathbb{E}[g(X)]$ transforms every possible value and then averages the transformed results. Thus, for a nonlinear function $g$,

$$
g(\mathbb{E}[X])\neq\mathbb{E}[g(X)]
$$

in general.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/expectation-of-functions.qmd
:::

Mathematical validity does not supply that theory.

::: {.notes}

## Linearity of expectation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: concept -->

Must we derive a new PMF for $X$ before finding its expectation?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The preceding page showed that a nonlinear transformation is ordinarily applied before its expectation is taken. A linear combination has an additional simplification. In a CMUdict pronunciation, total phone count $X$ is the sum of vowel-phone count $V$ and consonant-phone count $C$. Must we derive a new PMF for $X$ before finding its expectation?

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

## Linearity of expectation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: math -->

Basically, we can average each contribution and then add those averages. More specifically, **linearity of expectation** gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[V+C]
=\mathbb{E}[V]+\mathbb{E}[C].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, we can average each contribution and then add those averages. More specifically, **linearity of expectation** gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[V+C]
=\mathbb{E}[V]+\mathbb{E}[C].
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/04-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: concept -->

Their sum is the empirical expected total, 6.381 phones.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The expected vowel and consonant contributions are 2.469 and 3.911 phones. Their sum is the empirical expected total, 6.381 phones.

[Sources]

## Stating the general rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: math -->

For random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[|X_i|]<\infty$ and constants $a_1,\ldots,a_n$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}[X_i].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[|X_i|]<\infty$ and constants $a_1,\ldots,a_n$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\mathbb{E}[X_i].
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

## Stating the general rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: math -->

For two variables and an added constant, this gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]
=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]+c.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For two variables and an added constant, this gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[aX+bY+c]
=a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]+c.
$$

## Stating the general rule

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/08-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: concept -->

The expectation operation passes through sums and constant multiples.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The expectation operation passes through sums and constant multiples.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

## Indicators {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: math -->

An indicator $I_A$ takes value one when event $A$ occurs and zero otherwise. Define $\pi_A\equiv p_{I_A}(1)$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[I_A]
&=0\times p_{I_A}(0)+1\times p_{I_A}(1)\\
&=\pi_A.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An indicator $I_A$ takes value one when event $A$ occurs and zero otherwise. Define $\pi_A\equiv p_{I_A}(1)$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[I_A]
&=0\times p_{I_A}(0)+1\times p_{I_A}(1)\\
&=\pi_A.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

## Independence is not required

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/11-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: concept -->

Linearity nevertheless holds because it concerns sums and marginal expectations, not products.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Vowel and consonant counts are associated across pronunciation entries. Their empirical covariance is 0.784 phones squared. Linearity nevertheless holds because it concerns sums and marginal expectations, not products.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

## Independence is not required {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation/12-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/linearity-of-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: f3cea73744419ff5261b667f9b175605b74f223f2ca3554e9214eb60c0de1cb0; role: math -->

The linear rule should not be extended to nonlinear operations. In general,

$$
\mathbb{E}[XY]
\neq\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].
$$

That product equality requires additional conditions.

::: {.notes}

## The Cauchy density {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: math -->

For $x_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\gamma>0$, write

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Cauchy}(x_0,\gamma)
$$

when $X$ has density

$$
f_X(x)
\equiv
\frac{1}{\pi\gamma
\left[1+\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\gamma}\right)^2\right]},
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $x_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\gamma>0$, write

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Cauchy}(x_0,\gamma)
$$

when $X$ has density

$$
f_X(x)
\equiv
\frac{1}{\pi\gamma
\left[1+\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\gamma}\right)^2\right]},
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

[Sources]

## Checking the two sides before combining them {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/08-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: math -->

Consider the positive part:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^b \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)}\,\mathrm dx
&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\log(1+b^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Consider the positive part:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^b \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)}\,\mathrm dx
&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\log(1+b^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

## Checking the two sides before combining them {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: math -->

Here they cannot, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
$$

is undefined.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

As $b\to\infty$, this quantity diverges to $+\infty$. By symmetry, the integral over the negative half-line diverges to $-\infty$. An expectation exists only when these two parts can be combined without making the result depend on how the limits are taken. Here they cannot, so

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
$$

is undefined.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd
:::

For every finite $b>0$,

$$
\int_{-b}^{b}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx=0.
$$

\int_{-b}^{b}x f_X(x)\,\mathrm dx=0.

## Principal value is not expectation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/12-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: concept -->

The principal value is not $\mathbb{E}[X]$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Taking the symmetric limit produces a Cauchy principal value of zero. An expectation is not defined by forcing the positive and negative truncation bounds to approach infinity at the same rate. It requires the probability-weighted integral itself to exist. Thus the principal value is not $\mathbb{E}[X]$.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd
:::

## Finite samples do not repair the model expectation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/13-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: concept -->

We compare running means from two procedures: bootstrap draws from the observed duration distribution and simulated draws from the data-calibrated Cauchy reference.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Every finite sample of Cauchy draws has a finite arithmetic mean, but that fact does not imply that the distribution has an expected value. We compare running means from two procedures: bootstrap draws from the observed duration distribution and simulated draws from the data-calibrated Cauchy reference.

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail/19-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/when-expectations-fail.qmd; note-sha256: 606e7078b716ee2838b1280b6a4ca5bf42cc5292a8f28395597dd766ab2cafa1; role: answer -->

## Variance and covariance

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: concept -->

We now measure spread in the CMUdict total phone-count distribution and then ask how vowel and consonant counts vary together.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The expected value page summarized the center of a distribution. But the mean does not say how tightly probability is concentrated around that center. We now measure spread in the CMUdict total phone-count distribution and then ask how vowel and consonant counts vary together.

## Variance and covariance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: math -->

Basically, we need to average distance from the mean without letting positive and negative deviations cancel. The **variance** does this by summarizing expected squared distance:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, we need to average distance from the mean without letting positive and negative deviations cancel. The **variance** does this by summarizing expected squared distance:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right].
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Variance and covariance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: math -->

For the empirical PMF,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)
=\sum_x (x-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[X])^2\widehat p_X(x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the empirical PMF,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)
=\sum_x (x-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[X])^2\widehat p_X(x).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

The denominator is the number of CMUdict entries because this variance describes the complete finite release, rather than an external population sample.

## Variance and covariance

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/07-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: concept -->

The rare, long pronunciations contribute more than their small masses alone would suggest because variance squares their distances from the mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The rare, long pronunciations contribute more than their small masses alone would suggest because variance squares their distances from the mean.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Why square the deviations? {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/08-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: math -->

The expected signed deviation is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=0.
$$

the calculation verifies this identity up to floating-point precision.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The expected signed deviation is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=0.
$$

the calculation verifies this identity up to floating-point precision.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Why square the deviations?

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/09-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: concept -->

Variance is thus sensitive to probability placed far from the mean.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Squaring prevents cancellation and gives greater weight to larger departures. Variance is thus sensitive to probability placed far from the mean.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Covariance and a variance decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/10-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: math -->

The **covariance** of vowel count $V$ and consonant count $C$ is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(V,C)
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(V-\mathbb{E}[V])(C-\mathbb{E}[C])\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **covariance** of vowel count $V$ and consonant count $C$ is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(V,C)
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(V-\mathbb{E}[V])(C-\mathbb{E}[C])\right].
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Covariance and a variance decomposition

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/11-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: concept -->

It does not by itself identify a phonological mechanism.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The empirical covariance is 0.784 phones squared. Positive covariance means that entries with more vowel phones tend also to contain more consonant phones, relative to their respective means. It does not by itself identify a phonological mechanism.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Covariance and a variance decomposition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/12-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: math -->

Because $X=V+C$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\operatorname{Var}[V]
+\operatorname{Var}[C]
+2\operatorname{Cov}(V,C).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Because $X=V+C$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\operatorname{Var}[V]
+\operatorname{Var}[C]
+2\operatorname{Cov}(V,C).
$$

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## Keeping the units visible

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/14-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: concept -->

Standard deviation takes a square root to return to the original units.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If phone count is measured in phones, each deviation is measured in phones. Squaring produces phones squared. Squared units make variance useful for algebra but less direct as a descriptive distance. Standard deviation takes a square root to return to the original units.

A variable can have a finite mean but place enough probability far from that mean for its variance to be infinite.

## Variance and covariance: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance/19-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 2ffb45e353f63c9066644c4037f539ee592c05fdd9d1d12fe52d9689c2807abe; role: answer -->

## Standard deviation {.section-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation/01-section; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd; note-sha256: 524c48d450e7b1d6880f111d391a29760aceb2c5d82bea9ba3344994a4d2fc74; role: section -->

<div class="source"><a href="https://github.com/cmusphinx/cmudict">CMUdict 0.7b</a></div>

## Standard deviation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd; note-sha256: 524c48d450e7b1d6880f111d391a29760aceb2c5d82bea9ba3344994a4d2fc74; role: concept -->

We answer with the CMUdict total phone counts.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The preceding page defined variance as an expected squared deviation from the mean. That squaring prevents cancellation, but it also changes the measurement units. How do we retain the spread information while returning to the original scale? We answer with the CMUdict total phone counts.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

## Standard deviation {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd; note-sha256: 524c48d450e7b1d6880f111d391a29760aceb2c5d82bea9ba3344994a4d2fc74; role: math -->

The **standard deviation** is the nonnegative square root of the variance:

$$
\sigma_X
\equiv
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]}.

## What standard deviation summarizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation/07-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd; note-sha256: 524c48d450e7b1d6880f111d391a29760aceb2c5d82bea9ba3344994a4d2fc74; role: concept -->

Squaring gives greater weight to large deviations, so the two summaries need not agree.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Standard deviation is the square root of the expected squared distance from the mean. It is not the average absolute distance from the mean. Squaring gives greater weight to large deviations, so the two summaries need not agree.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html
:::

## What standard deviation summarizes

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation/08-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/standard-deviation.qmd; note-sha256: 524c48d450e7b1d6880f111d391a29760aceb2c5d82bea9ba3344994a4d2fc74; role: concept -->

Equal means and standard deviations do not guarantee equal tails, symmetry, or modality.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Standard deviation is also not a complete description of distribution shape. Equal means and standard deviations do not guarantee equal tails, symmetry, or modality.

[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

The percentage is computed from CMUdict, not supplied by the definition of standard deviation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A fixed proportion of observations need not fall within one standard deviation of the mean. In this empirical PMF, 66.8% of pronunciation entries fall between 4.24 and 8.52 phones. The percentage is computed from CMUdict, not supplied by the definition of standard deviation.

## Central moments

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments.qmd; note-sha256: faa76e33971e737274cea29e591b3629f8b738e62f96ec48b77254af5f7ee18f; role: concept -->

Changing the exponent on the centered deviation gives a family of summaries sensitive to different aspects of that shape.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The preceding pages introduced variance and standard deviation. Variance summarizes squared deviations from the mean. But the empirical CMUdict phone-count distribution is asymmetric, with a small number of entries much farther above the mean than below it. Changing the exponent on the centered deviation gives a family of summaries sensitive to different aspects of that shape.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties
:::

## Central moments {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments.qmd; note-sha256: faa76e33971e737274cea29e591b3629f8b738e62f96ec48b77254af5f7ee18f; role: math -->

Basically, every member of this family centers first and then changes the power applied to the deviation. More specifically, the **$k$th central moment** of $X$ is

$$
\mu_k
\equiv\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^k\right],
$$

when this expectation exists.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Basically, every member of this family centers first and then changes the power applied to the deviation. More specifically, the **$k$th central moment** of $X$ is

$$
\mu_k
\equiv\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^k\right],
$$

when this expectation exists.

[Sources]

https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

## A moment does not determine a distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments/16-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments.qmd; note-sha256: faa76e33971e737274cea29e591b3629f8b738e62f96ec48b77254af5f7ee18f; role: concept -->

A central moment does not provide a complete account of distribution shape, and different distributions can share the same first several moments.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

An even power makes departures on both sides positive, while an odd power preserves direction. Increasing the power gives progressively more weight to values far from the mean. But a central moment does not provide a complete account of distribution shape, and different distributions can share the same first several moments.

[Sources]

Why is the first central moment zero whenever the mean exists?

Why is the first central moment zero whenever the mean exists?

## Central moments: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments/21-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/central-moments.qmd; note-sha256: faa76e33971e737274cea29e591b3629f8b738e62f96ec48b77254af5f7ee18f; role: answer -->

The first central moment is zero because $\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]=0$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The first central moment is zero because $\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]=0$.

## Categorical outcomes {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 8a6414ebde6693afbf280501ed784af738ed1e39198427d02540bbc5169d53eb; role: math -->

Let $L$ record interrogative lemma and let $\mathcal L$ be its finite support. A categorical probability vector $\boldsymbol\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K)$ satisfies $\pi_k\geq0$ and $\sum_k\pi_k=1$. We write

$$
L\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),
\qquad
p_L(\ell_k)=\mathbb{P}(L=\ell_k)=\pi_k.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $L$ record interrogative lemma and let $\mathcal L$ be its finite support. A categorical probability vector $\boldsymbol\pi=(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K)$ satisfies $\pi_k\geq0$ and $\sum_k\pi_k=1$. We write

$$
L\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi),
\qquad
p_L(\ell_k)=\mathbb{P}(L=\ell_k)=\pi_k.
$$

[Sources]

https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/tr_boun/
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-021-09558-0
https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11782
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 8a6414ebde6693afbf280501ed784af738ed1e39198427d02540bbc5169d53eb; role: math -->

The maximum-likelihood categorical probabilities are the empirical relative frequencies,

$$
\widehat\pi_k=\frac{n_k}{n}.
$$

## Binary outcomes {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: 8a6414ebde6693afbf280501ed784af738ed1e39198427d02540bbc5169d53eb; role: math -->

Define $O=1$ when the source relation is `obj` and $O=0$ when it is `nsubj`. Then

$$
O\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o},\quad o\in\{0,1\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Define $O=1$ when the source relation is `obj` and $O=0$ when it is `nsubj`. Then

$$
O\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o},\quad o\in\{0,1\}.
$$

## Mass, expectation, and variance {.equation-slide .small}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 97994d2c841119bcec8e0ad158e4e7ec34e14ffb515042654ead12a639d9b722; role: math -->

For $O\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o}.
$$

Because $O^2=O$, its expectation and variance follow directly:

$$
\mathbb{E}[O]=0(1-p)+1p=p,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[O]
&=\mathbb{E}[O^2]-\mathbb{E}[O]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $O\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(O=o)=p^o(1-p)^{1-o}.
$$

Because $O^2=O$, its expectation and variance follow directly:

$$
\mathbb{E}[O]=0(1-p)+1p=p,
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}[O]
&=\mathbb{E}[O^2]-\mathbb{E}[O]^2\\
&=p-p^2\\
&=p(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/bernoulli-distribution.qmd
:::

## The binomial distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 58e0f7719a7bcb1926a643b633af7cccb519792e76abf93031489bd68e9a5b1a; role: concept -->

If $n$ independent opportunities had the same object probability $p$, their sum would follow a **binomial distribution**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A Bernoulli variable records whether one Turkish interrogative argument is annotated as an object. If $n$ independent opportunities had the same object probability $p$, their sum would follow a **binomial distribution**.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 58e0f7719a7bcb1926a643b633af7cccb519792e76abf93031489bd68e9a5b1a; role: math -->

Let $O_1,\ldots,O_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ and $Y=\sum_{i=1}^n O_i$. Then

$$
Y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)
$$

with probability mass function

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y},
\qquad y\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $O_1,\ldots,O_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ and $Y=\sum_{i=1}^n O_i$. Then

$$
Y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)
$$

with probability mass function

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y},
\qquad y\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 58e0f7719a7bcb1926a643b633af7cccb519792e76abf93031489bd68e9a5b1a; role: math -->

Linearity of expectation and independence give

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=np,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=np(1-p).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Linearity of expectation and independence give

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=np,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=np(1-p).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 58e0f7719a7bcb1926a643b633af7cccb519792e76abf93031489bd68e9a5b1a; role: math -->

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y]
&=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^nO_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[O_i]
=np,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Y]
&=\operatorname{Var}[\sum_{i=1}^nO_i]
=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[O_i]
=np(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## The independence objection

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution/10-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 58e0f7719a7bcb1926a643b633af7cccb519792e76abf93031489bd68e9a5b1a; role: concept -->

It shows the distribution implied by the binomial assumptions and prepares us to recognize when those assumptions fail.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A potential worry is that the formula appears to model the corpus design. It does not. The BOUN extract contains tokens nested within sampled sentences, and its opportunity count was observed rather than fixed in repeated experiments. Thus the curve is a data-calibrated independent-trial reference. It shows the distribution implied by the binomial assumptions and prepares us to recognize when those assumptions fail.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/binomial-distribution.qmd

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The binomial distribution describes independent draws. A fixed sample drawn **without replacement** from a finite linguistic resource has less variation because each selected entry changes the composition of the remaining population. The **hypergeometric distribution** represents that design.

[Sources]

https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/
https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/
:::

## Mass, mean, and variance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/hypergeometric-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/hypergeometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c5748cc6996be4b710a35dbfa5f821adbd2beca164378d285626f04150d8ae81; role: math -->

If a population contains $N$ entries, $K$ carry a focal property, and $n$ entries are sampled without replacement, then the focal count $X$ has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\frac{\binom Kx\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If a population contains $N$ entries, $K$ carry a focal property, and $n$ entries are sampled without replacement, then the focal count $X$ has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\frac{\binom Kx\binom{N-K}{n-x}}{\binom Nn}.
$$

## Mass, mean, and variance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/hypergeometric-distribution/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/hypergeometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c5748cc6996be4b710a35dbfa5f821adbd2beca164378d285626f04150d8ae81; role: math -->

Its expectation is the same as that of a binomial count with $p=K/N$, but its variance contains the **finite-population correction**:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=n\frac KN,
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=n\frac KN\left(1-\frac KN\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Its expectation is the same as that of a binomial count with $p=K/N$, but its variance contains the **finite-population correction**:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=n\frac KN,
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=n\frac KN\left(1-\frac KN\right)\frac{N-n}{N-1}.
$$

## The geometric distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: concept -->

This is a **waiting count**: the number of failures before the first success.

::: {.notes}

The CMUdict sequence introduced pronunciation entries and their phone counts. We now ask how many consonants precede the first vowel phone in each entry. This is a **waiting count**: the number of failures before the first success.

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: math -->

If independent trials have constant success probability $p$, then

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(p)
$$

has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)=(1-p)^x p,
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If independent trials have constant success probability $p$, then

$$
X\sim\operatorname{Geometric}(p)
$$

has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)=(1-p)^x p,
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: math -->

Differentiating the geometric series or using its probability-generating function gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{1-p}{p},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Differentiating the geometric series or using its probability-generating function gives

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: math -->

To derive the mean, put $q=1-p$ and differentiate the geometric series:

$$
\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}q^x=\frac{1}{1-q},
\qquad
\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}=\frac{1}{(1-q)^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

To derive the mean, put $q=1-p$ and differentiate the geometric series:

$$
\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}q^x=\frac{1}{1-q},
\qquad
\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}=\frac{1}{(1-q)^2}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: math -->

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=p\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}xq^x\\
&=pq\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}\\
&=\frac{1-p}{p}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=p\sum_{x=0}^{\infty}xq^x\\
&=pq\sum_{x=1}^{\infty}xq^{x-1}\\
&=\frac{1-p}{p}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: math -->

The factorial moment $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]=2(1-p)^2/p^2$ then gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The factorial moment $\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]=2(1-p)^2/p^2$ then gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]+\mathbb{E}[X]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{1-p}{p^2}.
$$

$$

## Why the fit fails

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/12-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: concept -->

Matching a mean is thus not evidence that the family explains the observed shape.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The geometric process assumes independent phone positions with one constant vowel probability. English phonotactics, syllable structure, and the dictionary's lexical composition violate that process story. Matching a mean is thus not evidence that the family explains the observed shape.

[Sources]

## The geometric distribution: answer 2

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution/16-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/geometric-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: c7ce973404b4da64547105db8dcff85ac94214ee0c76c0679bbbf0960197bc87; role: answer -->

Differentiating $\ell(p)=n\log p+(\sum_i x_i)\log(1-p)$ and setting the derivative to zero gives $n/p-\sum_i x_i/(1-p)=0$, hence $\widehat p=1/(1+\overline X)$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## The negative-binomial distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 4359783d2214813305c687dfbbb5127dd8ee16824754f2062c67aec2c1d4123c; role: concept -->

For a pronunciation entry, let a vowel phone be a success and let $X$ count consonants before the third vowel.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The geometric distribution counts failures before the first success. The **negative-binomial distribution** counts failures before the $r$th success. For a pronunciation entry, let a vowel phone be a success and let $X$ count consonants before the third vowel.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 4359783d2214813305c687dfbbb5127dd8ee16824754f2062c67aec2c1d4123c; role: math -->

Under independent trials with constant success probability $p$,

$$
X\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(r,p)
$$

has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\binom{x+r-1}{x}(1-p)^x p^r,
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Under independent trials with constant success probability $p$,

$$
X\sim\operatorname{NegBin}(r,p)
$$

has mass

$$
\mathbb{P}(X=x)
=\binom{x+r-1}{x}(1-p)^x p^r,
\qquad x\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 4359783d2214813305c687dfbbb5127dd8ee16824754f2062c67aec2c1d4123c; role: math -->

The mean and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{r(1-p)}p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}.
$$

When $r=1$, these expressions reduce to the geometric distribution.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The mean and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{r(1-p)}p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}.
$$

When $r=1$, these expressions reduce to the geometric distribution.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 4359783d2214813305c687dfbbb5127dd8ee16824754f2062c67aec2c1d4123c; role: math -->

Writing $\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]$ yields the mean--variance form

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{r}
>\mu.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Writing $\mu=\mathbb{E}[X]$ yields the mean--variance form

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mu+\frac{\mu^2}{r}
>\mu.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 4359783d2214813305c687dfbbb5127dd8ee16824754f2062c67aec2c1d4123c; role: math -->

Thus every finite-$r$ member is overdispersed relative to a Poisson variable with the same mean. The family also contains a Poisson limit. If

$$
X_r\sim\operatorname{NegBin}\left(r,\frac{r}{r+\lambda}\right),
$$

then $\mathbb{E}[X_r]=\lambda$ and, for each nonnegative integer $x$,

$$
\lim_{r\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(X_r=x)
=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Thus every finite-$r$ member is overdispersed relative to a Poisson variable with the same mean. The family also contains a Poisson limit. If

$$
X_r\sim\operatorname{NegBin}\left(r,\frac{r}{r+\lambda}\right),
$$

then $\mathbb{E}[X_r]=\lambda$ and, for each nonnegative integer $x$,

$$
\lim_{r\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(X_r=x)
=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/negative-binomial-distribution.qmd
:::

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\frac{\lambda^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!},

and

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=\lambda,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=\lambda.
$$

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: bdc435e346e940fb9912e0034c71258ed1e82b861e09a17c934f457528f1eaac; role: math -->
