## Definition and fit {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution/08-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: bdc435e346e940fb9912e0034c71258ed1e82b861e09a17c934f457528f1eaac; role: math -->

For the present variable the exposure is one dative token, and the count is the number of recipient words beyond the first. The recurrence

$$
\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=y+1)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y)}
=\frac{\lambda}{y+1}
$$

shows how the mass increases up to the vicinity of $\lambda$ and decreases afterward.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For the present variable the exposure is one dative token, and the count is the number of recipient words beyond the first. The recurrence

$$
\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=y+1)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y)}
=\frac{\lambda}{y+1}
$$

shows how the mass increases up to the vicinity of $\lambda$ and decreases afterward.

[Sources]

https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/languageR/languageR_1.5.0.tar.gz
https://web.stanford.edu/~bresnan/qs-submit.pdf
:::

## Definition and fit {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/poisson-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: bdc435e346e940fb9912e0034c71258ed1e82b861e09a17c934f457528f1eaac; role: math -->

The log likelihood,

$$
\ell(\lambda)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[y_i\log\lambda-\lambda-\log(y_i!)\right],
$$

has derivative $\sum_i y_i/\lambda-n$, so $\widehat\lambda=\overline y$.

::: {.notes}

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 1d04b95de3b1f93f01fdc39d79bdcb07e766b5747d7282335f3b7a7e8eab5ef5; role: math -->

For $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a},&a\leq x\leq b,\\[4pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(a,b)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{b-a},&a\leq x\leq b,\\[4pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 1d04b95de3b1f93f01fdc39d79bdcb07e766b5747d7282335f3b7a7e8eab5ef5; role: math -->

Integrating the density gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12},
$$

and for $a\leq c<d\leq b$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(c\leq X\leq d)=\frac{d-c}{b-a}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The CDF is

$$
F_X(x)
=\begin{cases}
0,&x<a,\\
\dfrac{x-a}{b-a},&a\leq x\leq b,\\
1,&x>b.
\end{cases}
$$

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution/09-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 1d04b95de3b1f93f01fdc39d79bdcb07e766b5747d7282335f3b7a7e8eab5ef5; role: math -->

Integrating the first two raw moments gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b x\,\mathrm dx
=\frac{a+b}{2},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.
$$

Because this is a continuous distribution, $\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0$ for every exact point $x$, even where the density is positive.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

$$

$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\mathbb{E}[X^2]-\mathbb{E}[X]^2
=\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}.
$$

Because this is a continuous distribution, $\mathbb{P}(X=x)=0$ for every exact point $x$, even where the density is positive.

https://osf.io/sjefs/

## The uniform distribution: answer 4

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution/20-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/uniform-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 1d04b95de3b1f93f01fdc39d79bdcb07e766b5747d7282335f3b7a7e8eab5ef5; role: answer -->

The unit-interval support is appropriate because every value lies strictly between zero and one, but the flat density shape fails to match the concentration near zero.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The unit-interval support is appropriate because every value lies strictly between zero and one, but the flat density shape fails to match the concentration near zero. The beta distribution retains the bounded support while allowing the density shape to be estimated.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-017-0908-4
https://osf.io/sjefs/
:::

## The beta distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: concept -->

The **beta distribution** retains that support and estimates two shape parameters from the observations.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The uniform reference respected the unit-interval support of Provo modeled predictability but missed its shape. The **beta distribution** retains that support and estimates two shape parameters from the observations.

[Sources]

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: math -->

For $0<x<1$,

$$
f_X(x\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
       {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}
x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1},
\qquad \alpha,\beta>0.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $0<x<1$,

$$
f_X(x\mid\alpha,\beta)
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
       {\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}
x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1},
\qquad \alpha,\beta>0.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: math -->

The denominator is the beta function,

$$
B(\alpha,\beta)
=\int_0^1 t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,\mathrm dt
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The denominator is the beta function,

$$
B(\alpha,\beta)
=\int_0^1 t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,\mathrm dt
=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: math -->

It normalizes the numerator to unit area. The first two moments follow from beta-function recurrences:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\\
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
&=\frac{B(\alpha+2,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
=\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}
{(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

It normalizes the numerator to unit area. The first two moments follow from beta-function recurrences:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=\frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},\\
\mathbb{E}[X^2]
&=\frac{B(\alpha+2,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
=\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}
{(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: math -->

The mean and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\frac{\alpha\beta}
{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The mean and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]

{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}.
$$

## Definition

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/07-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: concept -->

The sum $\alpha+\beta$ is the **concentration**: at a fixed mean, larger concentration places more density near that mean.

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution/08-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 02023c73c5afe15c694464519db5c125c3c4e82ffd533a268ea0f2befeda3fe2; role: math -->

For an arbitrary finite interval $a<y<b$, the affine transformation $Y=a+(b-a)X$ has density

$$
f_Y(y)=\frac{1}{b-a}
f_X\!\left(\frac{y-a}{b-a}\right),
\qquad a<y<b.
$$

::: {.notes}

## The normal distribution {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: abde952de3f248b0536cf79e088cf14549f76f652635ecd8e078d0bcba87616f; role: concept -->

Its parameters should be estimated from the linguistic measurement at hand, and its shape should be compared with those observations rather than assumed from the name of the variable.

::: {.notes}

The **normal distribution** is a symmetric location-scale family. Its parameters should be estimated from the linguistic measurement at hand, and its shape should be compared with those observations rather than assumed from the name of the variable.

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: abde952de3f248b0536cf79e088cf14549f76f652635ecd8e078d0bcba87616f; role: math -->

For $X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For $X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
f_X(x)
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],
\qquad x\in\mathbb R.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: abde952de3f248b0536cf79e088cf14549f76f652635ecd8e078d0bcba87616f; role: math -->

The parameters are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[X]=\sigma^2.
$$

Because the centered distance is squared,

$$
f_X(\mu-d)=f_X(\mu+d).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The parameters are

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]=\mu,
\qquad

$$

Because the centered distance is squared,

$$

$$

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/normal-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: abde952de3f248b0536cf79e088cf14549f76f652635ecd8e078d0bcba87616f; role: math -->

Thus $\mu$ controls location while $\sigma$ controls scale. Standardization gives

$$
Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(X\leq x)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right),
$$

where

$$
\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-t^2/2}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

## The chi-squared distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: concept -->

Under an independent normal-sampling model, the uncertainty in an estimated variance has a **chi-squared reference distribution**.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The normal page estimated a mean and variance for each /i/ F1 speaker group. Under an independent normal-sampling model, the uncertainty in an estimated variance has a **chi-squared reference distribution**.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: math -->

If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_\nu$ are independent standard-normal variables, then

$$
Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2
\sim\chi^2_\nu.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $Z_1,\ldots,Z_\nu$ are independent standard-normal variables, then

$$
Q=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}Z_j^2
\sim\chi^2_\nu.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: math -->

Its density is

$$
f_Q(q)
=\frac{q^{\nu/2-1}e^{-q/2}}
       {2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)},
\qquad q>0,
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Q]=\nu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Q]=2\nu.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Its density is

$$
f_Q(q)
=\frac{q^{\nu/2-1}e^{-q/2}}
       {2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)},
\qquad q>0,
$$

with

$$
\mathbb{E}[Q]=\nu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Q]=2\nu.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: math -->

The moments follow from independence and the standard-normal moments:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\mathbb{E}[Z_j^2]
=\nu,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\operatorname{Var}[Z_j^2]
=2\nu.
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The moments follow from independence and the standard-normal moments:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\mathbb{E}[Z_j^2]
=\nu,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Q]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}\operatorname{Var}[Z_j^2]
=2\nu.
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: math -->

For an independent sample from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an independent sample from $\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$

## The chi-squared distribution: answer 4

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution/18-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/chi-squared-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: 8f51baa478f37e2e0cbc99bd568774bb966551cf5009e6195072676038e48711; role: answer -->

## The Student-t distribution

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: cd6f5361b828e4e62dd374dc81972d409e8e136146b8e5e2342a17e04f3a7f69; role: concept -->

Under independent normal sampling, the resulting statistic follows a **Student-$t$ distribution**, which has heavier tails than the standard normal.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Standardizing a sample mean with an estimated standard deviation adds uncertainty. Under independent normal sampling, the resulting statistic follows a **Student-$t$ distribution**, which has heavier tails than the standard normal.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd
:::

## Construction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: cd6f5361b828e4e62dd374dc81972d409e8e136146b8e5e2342a17e04f3a7f69; role: math -->

If $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $Q\sim\chi^2_\nu$, and $Z$ is independent of $Q$, then

$$
T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{Q/\nu}}\sim t_\nu.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $Q\sim\chi^2_\nu$, and $Z$ is independent of $Q$, then

$$
T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{Q/\nu}}\sim t_\nu.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd
:::

## Construction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: cd6f5361b828e4e62dd374dc81972d409e8e136146b8e5e2342a17e04f3a7f69; role: math -->

For independent normal differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ with population mean $\mu_D$,

$$
\overline D=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nD_i,
\qquad
S_D^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\overline D)^2,
$$

$$
T
=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For independent normal differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ with population mean $\mu_D$,

$$
\overline D=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nD_i,
\qquad
S_D^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\overline D)^2,
$$

$$
T
=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd
:::

## Construction {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/student-t-distribution.qmd; note-sha256: cd6f5361b828e4e62dd374dc81972d409e8e136146b8e5e2342a17e04f3a7f69; role: math -->

The centered differences obey

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\overline D)=0,
$$

so only $n-1$ deviations vary freely.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The centered differences obey

so only $n-1$ deviations vary freely.

The density is symmetric, $f_T(-t)=f_T(t)$, and for $c>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(|T|\geq c)=2\mathbb{P}(T\geq c).
$$

## Inverse-transform sampling

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 28685c90861b0c82fc9631eee1c4e64b52ea375ee63b171813eab60f13c4c480; role: concept -->

**Inverse-transform sampling** maps those uniform values into draws from the target PMF.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The empirical Turkish interrogative-lemma PMF assigns probability to labels, while a computer's basic random-number generator produces values on the unit interval. **Inverse-transform sampling** maps those uniform values into draws from the target PMF.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd

## From cumulative mass to labels {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 28685c90861b0c82fc9631eee1c4e64b52ea375ee63b171813eab60f13c4c480; role: math -->

For an ordered numerical support, define the generalized inverse CDF by

$$
F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\geq u\},
\qquad 0<u<1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For an ordered numerical support, define the generalized inverse CDF by

$$
F^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F(x)\geq u\},
\qquad 0<u<1.
$$

## From cumulative mass to labels

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling/04-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 28685c90861b0c82fc9631eee1c4e64b52ea375ee63b171813eab60f13c4c480; role: concept -->

That order does not imply that *hangi*, *kim*, and *ne* form a linguistic scale.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

If $U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$, then $F^{-1}(U)$ has CDF $F$. For categorical labels, we first assign a computational order. That order does not imply that *hangi*, *kim*, and *ne* form a linguistic scale.

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd

## From cumulative mass to labels {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd; note-sha256: 28685c90861b0c82fc9631eee1c4e64b52ea375ee63b171813eab60f13c4c480; role: math -->

The construction works because, at continuity points of $F$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(F^{-1}(U)\leq x\right)
=\mathbb{P}\!\left(U\leq F(x)\right)
=F(x).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The construction works because, at continuity points of $F$,

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(F^{-1}(U)\leq x\right)
=\mathbb{P}\!\left(U\leq F(x)\right)
=F(x).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/inverse-transform-sampling.qmd
:::

## Random seeds

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/random-seeds/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/random-seeds.qmd; note-sha256: e9194538c4ee1dc28ef1394f63b6fc774ab1483152121e7eb6651892986a11cb; role: concept -->

Reproducing a sequence is not the same as collecting a new linguistic sample.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A pseudorandom generator produces a deterministic sequence from an initial state. A **random seed** records that state, allowing a stochastic computation to be reproduced exactly. Reproducing a sequence is not the same as collecting a new linguistic sample.

## Joint distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 71a8020784eb7c72a981b4b6689a9e87487f4070cf26a1ca81e7676e4c51334b; role: concept -->

A **joint distribution** assigns mass to the ordered length pair and thus preserves which values co-occur.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Recipient length and theme length are measured on the same dative token. Separate distributions discard that pairing. A **joint distribution** assigns mass to the ordered length pair and thus preserves which values co-occur.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 71a8020784eb7c72a981b4b6689a9e87487f4070cf26a1ca81e7676e4c51334b; role: math -->

Let $R$ be recipient length in words and $T$ be theme length in words. Their joint PMF is

$$
p_{R,T}(r,t)
=\mathbb{P}(R=r,T=t).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $R$ be recipient length in words and $T$ be theme length in words. Their joint PMF is

$$
p_{R,T}(r,t)
=\mathbb{P}(R=r,T=t).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 71a8020784eb7c72a981b4b6689a9e87487f4070cf26a1ca81e7676e4c51334b; role: math -->

It must satisfy

$$
p_{R,T}(r,t)\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_r\sum_t p_{R,T}(r,t)=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

It must satisfy

$$
p_{R,T}(r,t)\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_r\sum_t p_{R,T}(r,t)=1.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 71a8020784eb7c72a981b4b6689a9e87487f4070cf26a1ca81e7676e4c51334b; role: math -->

For any set $A$ of length pairs,

$$
\mathbb{P}\big(\langle R,T\rangle\in A\big)
=\sum_{\langle r,t\rangle\in A}p_{R,T}(r,t).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For any set $A$ of length pairs,

$$
\mathbb{P}\big(\langle R,T\rangle\in A\big)
=\sum_{\langle r,t\rangle\in A}p_{R,T}(r,t).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd; note-sha256: 71a8020784eb7c72a981b4b6689a9e87487f4070cf26a1ca81e7676e4c51334b; role: math -->

For absolutely continuous variables, the corresponding definition is

$$
\mathbb{P}\big(\langle R,T\rangle\in A\big)
=\iint_A f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm dt,
$$

where $f_{R,T}(r,t)\geq0$ and $\iint_{\mathbb R^2}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm dt=1$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For absolutely continuous variables, the corresponding definition is

$$
\mathbb{P}\big(\langle R,T\rangle\in A\big)
=\iint_A f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm dt,
$$

where $f_{R,T}(r,t)\geq0$ and $\iint_{\mathbb R^2}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr\,\mathrm dt=1$.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd
:::

## Marginal distributions

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: concept -->

A **marginal distribution** removes one measurement by summing over all of its possible values.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A joint PMF preserves two paired measurements. A **marginal distribution** removes one measurement by summing over all of its possible values.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd

## Marginalization {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: math -->

For recipient length $R$ and theme length $T$,

$$
p_R(r)=\sum_t p_{R,T}(r,t),
\qquad
p_T(t)=\sum_r p_{R,T}(r,t).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For recipient length $R$ and theme length $T$,

$$
p_R(r)=\sum_t p_{R,T}(r,t),
\qquad
p_T(t)=\sum_r p_{R,T}(r,t).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd
:::

## Marginalization {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: math -->

Each marginal normalizes:

$$
\sum_r p_R(r)=1,
\qquad
\sum_t p_T(t)=1.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Each marginal normalizes:

$$
\sum_r p_R(r)=1,
\qquad
\sum_t p_T(t)=1.
$$

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: concept -->

Marginalization forgets the pairing but not the frequency of the retained variable.

## Marginalization {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: math -->

For a joint density, summation becomes integration:

$$
f_R(r)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dt,
\qquad
f_T(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a joint density, summation becomes integration:

$$
f_R(r)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dt,
\qquad
f_T(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{R,T}(r,t)\,\mathrm dr.
$$

## Marginalization {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/marginal-distributions.qmd; note-sha256: b00cb9145ee6481fcd847f5b74fe04877afd134288f46e51a208e4968c2a32ce; role: math -->

Marginalization should not be confused with conditioning. When $p_T(t)>0$,

$$
p_{R\mid T}(r\mid t)=\frac{p_{R,T}(r,t)}{p_T(t)},
$$

which fixes one value and renormalizes instead of summing it out.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Marginalization should not be confused with conditioning. When $p_T(t)>0$,

$$
p_{R\mid T}(r\mid t)=\frac{p_{R,T}(r,t)}{p_T(t)},
$$

which fixes one value and renormalizes instead of summing it out.

## Conditional independence

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd; note-sha256: 984d426b0ce6bf109be353f3d18b23a233e637ab44f350f326bd18b1054e15c0; role: concept -->

**Conditional independence** names the stronger claim that their conditional joint distribution factorizes within every value of the conditioning variable.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Two variables can remain associated even after a third variable is held fixed. **Conditional independence** names the stronger claim that their conditional joint distribution factorizes within every value of the conditioning variable.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd; note-sha256: 984d426b0ce6bf109be353f3d18b23a233e637ab44f350f326bd18b1054e15c0; role: math -->

Let $A$ record recipient pronominality, $B$ recipient realization, and $M$ corpus modality. We write

$$
A\perp B\mid M
$$

when, for every value with positive conditioning probability,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a,B=b\mid M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m)\,
 \mathbb{P}(B=b\mid M=m).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $A$ record recipient pronominality, $B$ recipient realization, and $M$ corpus modality. We write

$$
A\perp B\mid M
$$

when, for every value with positive conditioning probability,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a,B=b\mid M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m)\,
 \mathbb{P}(B=b\mid M=m).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd; note-sha256: 984d426b0ce6bf109be353f3d18b23a233e637ab44f350f326bd18b1054e15c0; role: math -->

Equivalently, wherever the conditioning probabilities are positive,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid B=b,M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Equivalently, wherever the conditioning probabilities are positive,

$$
\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid B=b,M=m)
=\mathbb{P}(A=a\mid M=m).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd
:::

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd; note-sha256: 984d426b0ce6bf109be353f3d18b23a233e637ab44f350f326bd18b1054e15c0; role: concept -->

This **conditional-invariance criterion** says that learning $B$ supplies no further information about $A$ after $M$ is known.

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd; note-sha256: 984d426b0ce6bf109be353f3d18b23a233e637ab44f350f326bd18b1054e15c0; role: math -->

For a contingency table within modality $m$, factorization predicts cell count

## Conditional expectation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: concept -->

A **conditional expectation** gives the mean within a specified condition.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A marginal mean averages across all dative tokens. If recipient length differs between NP and PP realizations, that average conceals structured variation. A **conditional expectation** gives the mean within a specified condition.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: math -->

For discrete $X$ and $Y$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]
=\sum_x x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid Y=y).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For discrete $X$ and $Y$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]
=\sum_x x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid Y=y).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: math -->

For a conditional density, the analogous definition is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,\mathrm dx.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For a conditional density, the analogous definition is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,\mathrm dx.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd
:::

## Definition

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: concept -->

The conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=m(Y)$ is itself a random variable: its value depends on the realized category of $Y$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Writing $m(y)=\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]$ makes the **conditional-mean function** explicit. The conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=m(Y)$ is itself a random variable: its value depends on the realized category of $Y$.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: math -->

The **law of total expectation** reconnects conditional and marginal means:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\sum_y \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]\mathbb{P}(Y=y).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **law of total expectation** reconnects conditional and marginal means:

$$
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\sum_y \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]\mathbb{P}(Y=y).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation/07-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-expectation.qmd; note-sha256: dba245a9fd921940edb7f5bfb7f1dcec56a6939dfe7f4949af29ef38c79d7850; role: math -->

Indeed, substituting the conditional PMF gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=\sum_x x\sum_y\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y)\\
&=\sum_y\left[
  \sum_x x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid Y=y)
  \right]\mathbb{P}(Y=y).
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Indeed, substituting the conditional PMF gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X]
&=\sum_x x\sum_y\mathbb{P}(X=x,Y=y)\\
&=\sum_y\left[
  \sum_x x\,\mathbb{P}(X=x\mid Y=y)
  \right]\mathbb{P}(Y=y).
\end{aligned}
$$

## Covariance

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: concept -->

The **covariance** summarizes whether their deviations from their respective means tend to have the same sign.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Recipient and theme lengths are paired on each dative token. The **covariance** summarizes whether their deviations from their respective means tend to have the same sign.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: math -->

For random variables $R$ and $T$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}\left[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])\right].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For random variables $R$ and $T$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}\left[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])\right].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: math -->

Expanding the product gives the equivalent identity

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Expanding the product gives the equivalent identity

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/05-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: math -->

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])]
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]
-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&\quad-\mathbb{E}[T]\mathbb{E}[R]
+\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])]
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]
-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&\quad-\mathbb{E}[T]\mathbb{E}[R]
+\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
\end{aligned}
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: math -->

For constants $a,b,c,d$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(aR+b,cT+d)
=ac\,\operatorname{Cov}(R,T).
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For constants $a,b,c,d$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(aR+b,cT+d)
=ac\,\operatorname{Cov}(R,T).
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd
:::

Here both lengths are measured in words, so covariance is measured in words squared.

## Sample covariance {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance/11-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/covariance.qmd; note-sha256: 16c022ab86c668d8230587210dc7ea30dd426138c542b70878949fff9f946756; role: math -->

$$

=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(R_i-\overline R)(T_i-\overline T).

=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(R_i-\overline R)(T_i-\overline T).

## Correlation

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/02-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: concept -->

**Correlation** divides covariance by both standard deviations, producing a unitless measure of linear association.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Covariance changes when either variable is rescaled. **Correlation** divides covariance by both standard deviations, producing a unitless measure of linear association.

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/03-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: math -->

For variables with positive finite variances,

$$
\rho_{R,T}
=\operatorname{Corr}(R,T)
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)}
{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[R]\operatorname{Var}[T]}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

For variables with positive finite variances,

$$
\rho_{R,T}
=\operatorname{Corr}(R,T)
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)}
{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[R]\operatorname{Var}[T]}}.
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd
:::

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/04-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: math -->

Equivalently, if

$$
Z_R=\frac{R-\mathbb{E}[R]}{\operatorname{SD}(R)},
\qquad
Z_T=\frac{T-\mathbb{E}[T]}{\operatorname{SD}(T)},
$$

then

$$
\rho_{R,T}=\mathbb{E}[Z_RZ_T].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Equivalently, if

$$
Z_R=\frac{R-\mathbb{E}[R]}{\operatorname{SD}(R)},
\qquad
Z_T=\frac{T-\mathbb{E}[T]}{\operatorname{SD}(T)},
$$

then

$$
\rho_{R,T}=\mathbb{E}[Z_RZ_T].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd
:::

## Definition

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/05-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: concept -->

The endpoints occur only under exact positive or negative linear dependence.

::: {.notes}

Cauchy--Schwarz implies $-1\leq\rho_{R,T}\leq1$. The endpoints occur only under exact positive or negative linear dependence.

## Definition {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/06-math; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: math -->

Correlation is symmetric, $\rho_{R,T}=\rho_{T,R}$. For nonzero $a$ and $c$,

$$
\operatorname{Corr}(aR+b,cT+d)
=\operatorname{sign}(ac)\operatorname{Corr}(R,T).
$$

::: {.notes}

Correlation is symmetric, $\rho_{R,T}=\rho_{T,R}$. For nonzero $a$ and $c$,

$$
\operatorname{Corr}(aR+b,cT+d)
=\operatorname{sign}(ac)\operatorname{Corr}(R,T).
$$

Positive unit conversions leave correlation unchanged, while reversing exactly one axis reverses its sign.

## What near-zero correlation does not establish

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/10-concept; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: concept -->

Nor does it license a causal conclusion about constituent planning.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A near-zero correlation rules out only a strong linear relation in this empirical table. It does not establish independence: the joint distribution can retain nonlinear structure, and both variables are associated with other properties of the construction. Nor does it license a causal conclusion about constituent planning.

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/16-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: answer -->

Multiplying recipient length by any positive conversion constant multiplies its covariance and standard deviation by the same factor, leaving the correlation at $0.031530$.

::: {.notes}

Multiplying recipient length by any positive conversion constant multiplies its covariance and standard deviation by the same factor, leaving the correlation at $0.031530$.

## Correlation: answer 4

<!-- generated-slide-id: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation/20-answer; notes-page: random-variables-and-distributions/correlation.qmd; note-sha256: d57390daec3e21b8f30a873f84b94e7cbbe14e5a5f37202572a2ea6af7e665ac; role: answer -->

A symmetric nonlinear relation such as $T=(R-\mathbb{E}[R])^2$ can be deterministic while having zero correlation with $R$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A symmetric nonlinear relation such as $T=(R-\mathbb{E}[R])^2$ can be deterministic while having zero correlation with $R$. This closes the distribution chapter. The statistical-inference chapter next asks what an observed sample can say about an unknown quantity.

[Sources]
